subject: Biotechnology
title: Patent Law and Biotech
description: A short lesson to help you apply Patent Law and Biotech.

hook.text: Can you patent a gene? In 2013 the Supreme Court said no to natural DNA — but yes to synthetic cDNA.

buildup.text: Myriad Genetics held patents on BRCA1 and BRCA2 — charging $3,000 for a breast cancer risk test no competitor could offer.

discovery.text: The Supreme Court ruled in AMP v. Myriad that isolated natural DNA is not patentable — it is a product of nature.

twist.text: CRISPR patent battles between the Broad Institute and UC Berkeley lasted a decade — billions hung on who invented it first.

climax.text: Patent pools and licensing agreements now share CRISPR access — collaboration replaces litigation for academic users.

punchline.text: Discover or invent? The line between nature and innovation defines biotech patents.

quiz.question: Why did the Supreme Court rule that isolated natural DNA cannot be patented?
options: DNA is too small to be considered an invention
Isolating a naturally occurring DNA sequence does not create anything new — it is a product of nature
The patent had already expired by the time the case was decided

details.summary: Biotechnology patents protect inventions including genes, engineered organisms, diagnostic methods, and therapeutic processes. The landmark Diamond v. Chakrabarty case in 1980 established that living organisms could be patented, enabling the biotech industry's commercial foundation.
details.whyItMatters: Patents drive biotech investment by guaranteeing returns on costly R&D. But they also restrict access and raise questions about patenting life itself.
takeaways: Living organisms can be patented since Diamond v. Chakrabarty in 1980
Naturally occurring genes cannot be patented but modified versions can
Patent terms of 20 years protect biotech investments in R&D

faq.question: Can human genes be patented?
faq.answer: Since the 2013 Supreme Court ruling in AMP v. Myriad Genetics, naturally occurring human genes cannot be patented. However, complementary DNA, engineered gene variants, and methods using genes can still be patented. This significantly changed genetic testing accessibility.

faq.question: How do patents affect drug prices in biotechnology?
faq.answer: Patents grant 20-year monopolies allowing companies to set high prices to recoup R&D costs. When patents expire, biosimilars enter the market at lower prices. Critics argue patents enable excessive pricing; proponents argue without them, innovation funding would collapse.
